doc.title: Al Chez interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, February 13, 2019

title: Iron chops, practice habits and playing America
summary: Chez describes growing up in drum and bugle corps playing long hours, compares keeping up trumpet chops to an athlete, and recalls playing America in the stadium.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: So you, sir, have a set of iron chops.

I don’t know if they’re iron. They hurt. You know that’s a, they hurt. I’ve been playing a long time and I grew up playing you know in the drum & bugle corps and the marching band activity, and I got used to playing for 12 hours a day really early on in my career and that kind of — I kind of kept that going you know. Hard work, you know, you want to cash a check do the work. You know what I mean? So there you go.
Isn’t there some saying about brass players like if you don’t practice one day you notice, two days the audiences notices, or something like that.

Well I’ve been on vacation so, you know no. Yeah you’ve got to, you know, I guess it’s like an athlete. Any athlete if you sit out, if an athlete goes on the disabled list he’s going to come back and he’s not going to be at his best. He’s going to have to go to the minor leagues or he’s going to have to go for a rehab a couple of games, and get his game back. I think it’s the same thing with playing the trumpet. You have to stay up on your game. You have to — it’s a full time job.
Is it also part of physically keeping your — I mean I’m thinking about your lung power. Because I just watched, about half an hour ago I watched you playing “America” in this stadium.
Oh that was, they asked me to do that about 15 minutes before I did it and I was like under the bleachers trying to figure out a good key.
Well it turned out to be a pretty high key also.

Yes it did, yes it did. So that was a lot of fun. That was a lot of fun. But yeah it’s pretty physical. Everything — it’s one of the reasons why I love playing the trumpet.
